title: How spirits are made
lead: Fermenting, distilling and aging: the three steps behind every bottle on the back bar.

read.bigIdea: Every spirit starts as something fermented.
read.where: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol. **Distilling** heats that liquid; alcohol boils before water, so the vapor is stronger than what went in. The start decides the spirit: **grain** for whiskey and most vodka, **agave** for tequila and mezcal, **sugarcane** for rum, **grapes or other fruit** for brandy.

read.bigIdea: Two kinds of still, two kinds of spirit.
read.where: A **pot still** works one batch at a time and is often run twice; more of the base’s flavor comes through. A **column still** runs nonstop and can reach a higher strength, so the spirit is lighter. Either way the distiller keeps the **heart** of the run and sets aside the first and last parts. Cognac, for example, is distilled twice in **copper pot stills**.

adds vanilla and spice, and softens the spirit.
is the age of the youngest spirit in the bottle.

read.bigIdea: The barrel adds color, flavor and time.
read.where: Spirits come off the still clear. Time in **oak** adds color and flavors like vanilla and spice, and softens the spirit. **New charred oak** gives a lot of flavor fast; **used casks** give less. An **age statement** is the age of the **youngest** spirit in the bottle. Some whiskies may add plain caramel color.
read.mixup: A 12-year-old whisky can hold older whisky, but **nothing younger than 12 years**.

read.bigIdea: Proof is twice the ABV, in the US.
read.where: **ABV** is the share of alcohol in the bottle. In the US, **proof** is twice the ABV: 40% is 80 proof. US whiskey is bottled at **40% or more**; in the EU, gin, vodka and rum are at least **37.5%**. **Cask strength** means bottled at about the strength it came out of the barrel, with little or no water added.
